overview:
In Jain philosophy, **omniscience (kevala‑jñāna)** is the perfected state of knowledge attained by an *arihant* or *kevalin* who has completely eliminated the obscuring karmas. It is not merely vast knowledge but the total, direct, and non-mediated apprehension of all substances (*dravya*), their modes (*paryāya*), and their infinite temporal modifications across past, present, and future. Jainism treats omniscience as a definable epistemic condition grounded in its karma theory and metaphysics, not as an abstract theological claim.

Jain thinkers describe omniscience as arising when the **four knowledge-obscuring karmas**—*jñānāvaraṇa*, *darśanāvaraṇa*, *mohanīya*, and *antarāya*—are destroyed. At this moment, the soul’s inherent luminosity manifests fully. The kevalin perceives reality directly, without sensory dependence, inference, or scriptural testimony. This state is associated with the **13th gunasthāna** (stage of spiritual development), immediately preceding liberation.

Across Jain traditions, omniscience is treated with careful philosophical rigor. Digambara texts emphasize the kevalin’s non-activity and complete detachment, while Śvetāmbara sources describe the kevalin as continuing to teach through a divine sound (*divya‑dhvani*). Despite these differences, both traditions agree that omniscience is a natural property of the liberated soul and arises through the destruction of karmic bondage.

Modern scholarship highlights Jainism’s distinctive contribution to global epistemology: omniscience is not framed as supernatural revelation but as the soul’s natural state once obstructions are removed. The concept is tightly linked to Jain ethics, nonviolence, and disciplined practice, which gradually weaken karmic influx and support the soul’s ascent toward perfect knowledge.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārtha Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti/Umāsvāmi
primary_sources.translation: Omniscience arises from the destruction of karmas.
primary_sources.notes: Tattvārtha Sūtra 10.1 is one of the most cited aphorisms defining omniscience. The text is accepted across Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions (Corpus Tier A).

primary_sources.title: Samavāyāṅga Sūtra
primary_sources.author: Attributed to early Śvetāmbara canonical compilers
primary_sources.notes: A canonical Śvetāmbara text describing the scope of omniscience. The phrase appears in discussions of the qualities of perfected beings (Corpus Tier A).

primary_sources.title: Ṣaṭkhaṅḍāgama
primary_sources.author: Kundakunda lineage (Digambara)
primary_sources.translation: One who has reached the state of complete purity becomes a kevalin.
primary_sources.notes: A foundational Digambara canonical text emphasizing the destruction of karmic impurities as the cause of omniscience (Corpus Tier A).

primary_sources.title: Gommatasāra Jīvakāṇḍa
primary_sources.author: Nemichandra Siddhānta Chakravartin
primary_sources.notes: A classical Digambara commentary describing the infinite nature of kevala‑jñāna (Corpus Tier B).

misconceptions.myth: Omniscience in Jainism means knowing only spiritual truths or moral principles.
misconceptions.reality: Jain omniscience encompasses all substances, modes, and temporal modifications—cosmology, matter, souls, karma, and every event across time. It is a total epistemic state, not limited to spiritual insight.

misconceptions.myth: Omniscience is a miraculous or supernatural gift granted by a deity.
misconceptions.reality: Jainism teaches that omniscience is the soul’s natural state once knowledge‑obscuring karmas are destroyed. No external divine intervention is involved.

misconceptions.myth: Different Jain traditions disagree on whether omniscience is possible.
misconceptions.reality: All major Jain traditions—Digambara, Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka, Sthānakavāsī, and Terāpanth—affirm the reality of omniscience. Their differences concern the kevalin’s activities, not the existence of omniscience.
